transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Evan Park (NeoAI CTO), Sofia Martinez (NeoAI ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (NeoAI PM)

Summary:
- Intro / context: NeoAI evaluating Redwood for a PLG/self-serve integration with potential Dedicated pilot for production.
- Main concerns: time-to-first-token, free credits for trial, latency vs cost trade-offs, security (SOC2/KMS/VPC), and benching on their prompt distribution.
- Agreed next steps: quickstart resources, security docs, free credits, schedule technical demo/bench session.

Topics Covered:
- PLG quickstart, SDKs, free credits
- Hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem)
- Time-to-first-token and SDK integration patterns
- Security/compliance: SOC2, KMS, audit logs, SSO
- Pilot scoping and success criteria

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining — I'm Jordan from Redwood, with Maya our solutions engineer. How are you all doing?
[00:08] Evan: Good thanks, excited to learn more — short on time so we'll try to keep it tight.
[00:12] Maya: Great, quick agenda, we want to cover the PLG quickstart flow, free credits, how fast you can go from sign-up to first token, and then map that to your infra questions like Dedicated and VPC stuff.
[00:25] Liam: Sounds good. We're mostly curious about two things: how fast the dev experience is for our product teams, and how easy it is to graduate to a Dedicated capacity when we need predictable latency.
[00:36] Sofia: Also security — we have strict data residency and want to know about encryption and key management.
[00:41] Jordan: Totally. Quick high level: most teams start on the hosted Redwood API — simple REST/SDK, free credits to experiment, and you can prototype in hours. When you're ready you can reserve Dedicated capacity or go Private with a VPC/on-prem control plane. We'll show the quickstart flow and then talk about the Dedicated ramp.
[01:00] Evan: Can you walk through the time-to-first-token? We ran into friction with other providers where SDK install plus auth took too long.
[01:08] Maya: Absolutely. Typical flow is sign-up -> API key -> SDK example. With our quickstart repo you can run a curl or Python snippet in under 10 minutes. Realistically for a dev to get a token from their app it's about 20-30 minutes if they set up env vars and a simple call.
[01:25] Sofia: Is there an auth flow for teams? We use SSO and need SAML for access control.
[01:31] Jordan: Yes we support SSO/SAML for the Console. For API keys we also have scoped keys and RBAC in the console — you can rotate keys, set quotas, and bind keys to projects.
[01:45] Liam: Nice. For the free credits you mentioned — how does that work? We want to let product devs experiment without credit card friction.
[01:52] Jordan: We can provision a trial account with $2k in credits tied to your org; you can share invites with the team. We'll also provide sample prompts and a repo so folks can hit first token quickly.
[02:05] Evan: Great, that helps. On the Dedicated side — our main blocker is predictable 99p latency under 100ms for short prompts; is that realistic?
[02:15] Maya: There's some nuance — model and prompt size matter a lot. With smaller open models and an optimized Dedicated pool we've seen 95–120ms for single-token latencies depending on batch configs and sequence length. You can tune batching and caching; Dedicated gives more consistent tails because capacity is reserved.
[02:33] Evan: So we'd have to pick model variants? We care about both cost and generation quality.
[02:38] Maya: Yup, you can route between variants by policy — e.g., hosted low-cost model for non-prod, Dedicated higher-quality model in prod. Our Console shows per-route cost/latency so you can make tradeoffs.
[02:50] Sofia: For data security, we need clarity on KMS, encryption at rest, and audit logs — also whether logs leave our region.
[02:58] Jordan: We support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for Private and Dedicated. Hosted has encryption at rest and in transit by default; for stricter requirements we recommend Private with VPC. Audit logs and request-level tracing are available with retention options. We'll send the security pack.
[03:15] Liam: Any gotchas about onboarding? For example, model size or tokenization differences that break our current prompts?
[03:23] Maya: Some tokenization differences exist between models — we include tokenizer tools in the repo and examples to normalize. Also be mindful of context window sizes when you port prompts across models.
[03:35] Evan: We plan to run a quick POC: stage 1 PLG integration to test adoption; stage 2 a Dedicated pilot for traffic spikes. Timeline — we'd like to start trial this week and evaluate in 2–3 weeks.
[03:47] Jordan: That aligns well with our typical flow. We'll give you quickstart materials and $2k credits. If you can share expected QPS and prompt distributions we'll propose a Dedicated config for a pilot.
[03:58] Sofia: One more question on logs — are request logs stored with customer data? We need to ensure PII isn't kept.
[04:04] Maya: By default logs are kept for diagnostic purposes but you can opt out or configure redaction. For Private deployments audit logs live in your VPC and you control retention.
[04:14] Evan: Cool. Can you also run a short benchmark for our prompt set?
[04:18] Jordan: Yes, that's part of the next step. We'll schedule a 45-minute benchmark session where Maya will run tests with your prompts against a few model variants and a Dedicated config.
[04:28] Liam: If we do Dedicated, is there an autoscale or burst option?
[04:31] Maya: Yes, Dedicated supports autoscaling policies and burst capacity. You can set a baseline reserved pool and allow short bursts to shared capacity or fallback to hosted if the pool fills.
[04:42] Evan: Pricing model for Dedicated — is it a commit? monthly?
[04:45] Jordan: Typically it's reserved monthly/annual capacity with a commit; we do month-to-month pilots for evaluation. We can share a pilot pricing proposal.
[04:53] Sofia: Any compliance certifications? SOC2 is a must for us.
[04:56] Maya: We have SOC2 Type II; we'll share the attestation and the compliance pack. For regulated workloads we recommend Private deployments.
[05:05] Evan: Latency targets — what does the Console show for per-route breakdown?
[05:09] Maya: The Console gives token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-request traces, and error analytics. That helps identify if latency is in the model compute or network.
[05:18] Liam: About time-to-first-token from origin — do you have SDK caching or connection warm-up to reduce cold start?
[05:24] Maya: We use persistent connections and the SDK supports streaming so the first token can arrive faster; KV cache and prefix caching also help for repeated prompts.
[05:33] Evan: Ok, we may want to do a short integration test: simple chat endpoint hitting a Redwood hosted API and see end-to-end latency from our EU region.
[05:41] Jordan: We can spin that up and provide region-specific endpoints. We'll note EU region for the trial.
[05:46] Sofia: Data residency — can hosted keep data in EU-only?
[05:49] Maya: Hosted supports regional endpoints; for strict residency Private is recommended. We'll include region placement details.
[05:57] Liam: Do you have any reference customers in fintech or healthcare?
[06:01] Jordan: Yes, we have several mid-market fintech customers using Dedicated with Private networking — we can share anonymized case studies.
[06:08] Evan: Great. Let's talk about success criteria for the pilot — what should we measure?
[06:12] Maya: We recommend: 1) time-to-first-token for a representative prompt set, 2) 99p latency under expected load, 3) cost per generated token, and 4) quality metrics (human evals on output).
[06:23] Liam: For quality metrics, we'll supply a few eval prompts.
[06:27] Jordan: Perfect. If you share them we'll baseline quality across a couple of open models and a Redwood-verified variant.
[06:34] Sofia: One more operational question — how are model rollouts handled? We need canary and automatic fallback.
[06:40] Maya: We support canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic fallback policies to a compatible model variant if a rollout fails. You can configure these in the Console per-route.
[06:50] Evan: About cost control — can we set quotas per team?
[06:53] Jordan: Yes per-project quotas and rate limits; also token-level budgeting and alerts.
[06:59] Liam: Any integration with our existing observability stack?
[07:02] Maya: We provide tracing hooks and exportable logs to common destinations (S3, Datadog, Splunk).
[07:08] Evan: Ok great. Anything else we should know about PLG onboarding?
[07:12] Jordan: The Quickstart repo includes sample apps, a Postman collection, SDK snippets, and a short tutorial — most teams get meaningful results in a day.
[07:21] Sofia: Cool. If we run into tokenization issues, who do we loop in?
[07:25] Maya: Loop me in — I'll help with tokenizer scripts and prompt normalization.
[07:29] Evan: Recap and next steps?
[07:32] Jordan: Recap: we'll provision $2k trial credits, send the quickstart repo and security pack, schedule a 45-min benchmark/demo week of 12/14, and Maya will prepare a pilot Dedicated config once you share QPS and prompt sets.
[07:47] Liam: Sounds good.
[07:49] Evan: Thanks, appreciate it.
[07:51] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up by EOD with the materials.

Note: transcription includes typical auto-caption noise; names and some product terms may be slightly garbled in the raw capture. Shared artifacts: Quickstart repo: https://redwood.example.com/quickstart/neoai, Security pack link: https://redwood.example.com/security/pack (will send directly), Sample prompt spreadsheet (shared in follow-up).
